claims.text: A threshold concentration of a reactive element such as Al enables high-entropy alloys to achieve high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The relevant Al threshold is approximately greater than 3–5 at.%.
The oxidation resistance arises through formation of a coherent, self-healing Al2O3 layer.
High configurational entropy of the alloy matrix retards oxygen diffusion.
Preferential oxidation of Al produces a continuous, adherent scale that limits subsequent oxidation.
The protective scale forms a nanostructured, coherent interface with the high-entropy matrix.
High entropy minimizes localized oxygen-diffusion channels in the Al-containing alloy.
Selective oxidation of Al is thermodynamically favored under the proposed oxidation conditions.
Selective Al oxidation yields a dense, slow-growing alumina scale.
Sluggish diffusion in the high-entropy matrix retards further oxygen ingress.
Interfacial coherence gives the alumina scale self-healing properties.
Relative to an Al-deficient baseline, the Al-containing alloy will form a more uniform and adherent alumina scale.
Relative to the baseline, the Al-containing alloy will exhibit lower mass gain and a slower oxide-growth rate.
The Al-deficient baseline will form a porous, non-protective mixture of oxides with a higher oxidation rate.
The proposed mechanism applies in air at approximately 900–1100°C for exposure times up to 100 hours.
